title: Northern Songs is formed | 1963
content:
The Beatles’ publishing company Northern Songs was formed on 22 February 1963.

Initially a limited company, it was created by the band’s manager Brian Epstein and music publisher Dick James to publish songs by John Lennon and Paul McCartney. The unusual setup was an effort by James, who had achieved only limited success as a publisher, to keep Lennon and McCartney signed to his company, and he managed that by offering them a more attractive deal than the standard one given to songwriters.

It was common at the time for composers to receive 50% of the performing rights, 50% of mechanical royalties, and 10% of sheet music revenue. By offering them a better rate, James ensured his future fortune as The Beatles became world famous. It was a minor leap of faith, but the initial costs were little more than those required to set up the new company.

James owned 49 shares, Lennon and McCartney had 19 and 20 respectively, and Epstein’s company NEMS was allocated the remaining 10. Dick James Music was also appointed to administer Northern Songs, which allowed it to take a further 10% of the company’s gross receipts.

The company was an almost instant success. James replicated it with Epstein’s other acts, creating Pacermusic for Gerry Marsden of Gerry and the Pacemakers, and Jaep Music Co to handle Epstein’s other NEMS acts. Jaep published George Harrison’s first composition, ‘Don’t Bother Me’.

Although Harrison founded his own publishing company, Mornyork Ltd, in September 1964, changing the name to Harrisongs Ltd in December, he signed a three-year contract with Northern Songs in 1965. When that expired in 1968, Harrison’s future Beatles songs were published by Harrisongs. Ringo Starr also formed a publishing company for his songs, Startling Music, in 1968.

James also set up Maclen Music Inc in America, Northern Songs (Pty) Ltd in Australia, and Northern Songs SARL in France.

In 1965 Northern Songs was floated on the London Stock Exchange, to reduce the income tax burdens of the initial owners. A quarter of the new shares – 1.25 million – were traded at an initial price of 66 pence. After the floatation, Lennon and McCartney each owned 750,000 (15%), NEMS had 375,000 (7.5%), Harrison and Starr each had 40,000 (1.6%). Dick James Music had 7.5%, and James and his lawyer Charles Silver each controlled 15%.

At the point of floatation, Northern Songs was valued at £2.7 million. The previous owners each sold a quarter of their holdings, and Lennon and McCartney each received £94,270 tax-free for the sale. However, it meant the company was at risk of a majority takeover, which duly happened in 1969 when James and Silver sold their shares to Associated Television for £1,525,000 without warning The Beatles or offering the chance to buy them instead. This move meant that the songs of Lennon-McCartney were for many years owned by ATV.
